title: Lesson 65: Fine-tuning in Practice: Datasets, LoRA, Evaluation, and Pitfalls
description: The practical manual for running a fine-tune well: shaping a fifty-to-one-hundred example teaching dataset as JSONL chat messages, adapting a model cheaply with LoRA by freezing the base and training low-rank update matrices, proving the change on an immutable held-out evaluation set, and the data and scope failures that sink projects.

questions.question: A team is preparing a supervised fine-tuning set to install a specific behavior. Which data choice gives the model the best chance of learning it?
options: A small set of realistic examples drawn from production prompts, paired with desired outputs.
A large set of scraped examples, on the theory that more data always improves a tune.
A set generated entirely by a weaker model so every example shares one uniform style.
A single long document describing the desired behavior in prose rather than in example pairs.
questions.explanation: The tuned model is bounded by the quality of its examples, so a small, clean, representative set paired with human ground truth beats a large noisy one. Quantity alone does not teach a behavior the examples never demonstrate.

questions.question: Full fine-tuning updates every weight in a large model. What does low-rank adaptation do instead to make the adaptation affordable?
options: It retrains the entire model on a smaller slice of the data at each step.
It removes most layers from the model so fewer weights exist to update.
It freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank update matrices.
It replaces the base model with a fixed lookup table of stored responses.
questions.explanation: Low-rank adaptation holds the original weights fixed and learns a compact update expressed as the product of two much smaller matrices. Because those matrices carry far fewer parameters, the training fits on modest hardware.

questions.question: A team wants the evaluation of a fine-tune to be trustworthy. Which practice supports that goal?
options: Judging the tune by how smoothly the training run progressed and how low its training loss fell.
Reusing a few evaluation examples during training so the model recognizes them and scores well.
Relying on the platform's automated safety checks as the only measure of quality.
Comparing the tuned model to the base model on a held-out set kept out of training.
questions.explanation: Evaluation has to be set up before training and must rely on a held-out set that never enters the data, with the tuned model compared to the base model on that same set. Training loss and a smooth run say nothing about whether the model generalizes.
